strait-of-hormuz.summary: Effectively closed to normal commercial traffic since 28 Feb: Iran requires permits and fees through its Strait Authority, a US blockade of Iranian ports has been in force since 14 July, and attacks on ships continue. The IMO recorded 9 tanker attacks in the strait in the week of 28 Sep-5 Oct, the highest weekly total since the war began; a chemical tanker (Acers) was separately struck by projectiles on 7 Oct about 51 nautical miles off Qatar, west of the usual attack cluster, and Iran's IRGC said it struck the LPG tanker NV Sunshine on 9 Oct for taking an unauthorized route (IRGC claim, unverified). Reuters reported, citing officials close to Tehran, that Iran plans to widen threats against ships using routes it hasn't authorized, including Omani-side channels and Gulf of Oman transfer points — a plan that could not be independently verified. President Trump said on 8 Oct the US will not attack Iran before November's midterm elections, that the US blockade remains in force, and that oil is flowing through the strait; he rejected Iran's latest proposal to end the war. Saudi Aramco is in talks to formalize long-term shuttle contracts built on the ship-to-ship transfer system that bypasses the strait, and VLCC freight on the Gulf-to-Asia route hit a record near $1.4 million/day as that shuttle system strains vessel supply. Kpler ship-tracking data put Hormuz crude exports at about 8.5 mb/d (roughly 40% below pre-war) in the week to 7 Oct, down from the 13.2 mb/d (about 77% of baseline) Kpler reported for the week to 29 Sep, even as satellite imagery had shown a 'major operational recovery' at Saudi Arabia's Yanbu terminal; Vortexa separately put non-Iranian Gulf oil flows at 81% of pre-war levels in September. Tankers still move mainly under naval escort or shuttle arrangements rather than normal free transit, and many sail with transponders off, so independent counts remain partial; IMF PortWatch's AIS-tracked tanker count for Hormuz averaged just 0.6/day in the week to 11 Oct, down from 1.3/day in late September, though broader tracking shows higher flows since many vessels sail dark. The attack zone widened further on 9 October when the fully laden VLCC GEM NO.2 was struck by an unidentified projectile about 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera, UAE, outside the strait itself; two more unnamed outbound tankers were then hit by projectiles and caught fire inside the strait on 10 and 11 October, per UKMTO, with crews reported safe in both cases. Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said on 11 October that the US response to Iran's seven conditions for reopening the strait was ‘insufficient’ and that Tehran would stop responding through the current channel; the US had replied via Qatari intermediaries. Delayed UKMTO and JMIC reports disclosed on 12 Oct showed the 11 Oct toll was larger than first known: six vessels, five tankers and a container ship, were struck that day, the highest single-day total since the war began; one was hit by a drone at Oman's Sohar anchorage and reclassified from 'suspicious activity' to an attack, and JMIC raised its threat assessment for the strait to SEVERE. No group claimed responsibility for any of the six. On 13 October the Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride sank after a projectile strike (21 crew safe; Iran's unevidenced naval-mine claim was disputed by maritime security firm Marisks), its sister ship GFS Giselle was damaged but reached anchorage, and the bulk carrier Cape Dao — struck 23 September — also went down; the IMO has documented more than 100 confirmed incidents and at least 24 seafarer deaths in the strait since the war began. CENTCOM said on 14 October it had destroyed an Iranian-affiliated dhow in the Gulf of Oman on 6 October, alleging it was helping target US Navy ships (CENTCOM claim, unverified). On 15 October CENTCOM said the US and regional partners "control the strait as commercial vessels continue to transit," citing more than 40 commercial transits in the prior 24 hours (CENTCOM claim, unverified); the JMIC advisory for 11-14 October counted about 121 US-facilitated transits, roughly 30 a day and about 22% of the ~138/day pre-war average, and said US forces had redirected 135 commercial vessels and disabled four as of 10-11 October. The IMO put the cumulative toll at 113 confirmed incidents and at least 24 seafarer deaths in the strait since the war began as of 14 October; JMIC separately logged 149 confirmed vessel incidents region-wide since 1 March, including eight projectile attacks on four tankers and four containerships on 11 and 13 October and a separate strike near Sohar, Oman, that left two crew of the tanker Petro Dolphin missing. UKMTO's weekly overview (16 Oct) said most vessels struck in the region are not reporting incidents to it, logged 12 further attacks in its latest period (10 in the strait, one each in the Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman), and counted only 254 transits in the week to 14 October (70% below pre-war levels) — of which just 42 were directly AIS-tracked, the rest being unverifiable US-reported 'facilitated' transits. CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said on 16 October that about 400 merchant ships transited in the same week and that US forces helped move over 100 million barrels of crude (CENTCOM claim, unverified), a figure UKMTO's own count cannot confirm; Iran's army chief Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami said on 15 October the strait would stay closed until Iran's rights are respected (Iranian claim, unverified). Reuters separately reported, citing tracking group UANI and satellite analysis firm SynMax, that Iran has shipped at least 4.1 million barrels of LPG on eight tankers and one jet-fuel cargo (to Myanmar in September) past the US blockade since mid-July, even as Iran's own crude exports fell to zero in September for the first time since Kpler began tracking the country in 2013. Gulf-to-China VLCC freight rates eased about 8% week on week to 776 Worldscale by 16 October, still near record highs, as Middle East demand cooled and Washington weighed easing shadow-fleet tanker sanctions. UKMTO reported that two tankers were struck 68 and 78 nautical miles northeast of al-Jubail, Saudi Arabia on 16 October, outside the strait itself, which ISW/CTP assessed was likely the work of the IRGC Navy; Iran's Revolutionary Guards separately said the ships, each carrying about 2 million barrels of crude, hit naval mines on an unauthorized route (IRGC claim, unverified; no independent confirmation per Reuters). Vitol's Asia head said on 16 October that a shortage of high-sulfur fuel oil for ships will persist even as Hormuz crude flows rise, as Gulf fuel-oil exports fall and refiners favor higher-margin diesel. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on 17 October that two more tankers, each carrying about 2 million barrels of crude, caught fire after hitting naval mines in the strait with their tracking switched off (IRGC claim, unverified; Reuters found no independent confirmation). On 18 October Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran's offer to reopen the strait within seven days of a US acceptance, first made in mid-September, still stands; the US has replied via Qatari mediators, but the two sides remain stuck on Washington's demand that Iran also address its nuclear program. Separately on 18 October, Turkey's energy minister said Ankara will take some of the diesel Russia is supplying under the Trump-Putin deal, after Russia curtailed exports. A tugboat was damaged by two unknown projectiles northeast of Khor Fakkan, UAE on 18 October, injuring one crew member before it continued its route; ISW/CTP assessed Iran likely carried out the strike. On 19 October Bloomberg reported Iran's oil-loading terminals have sat idle since late August, the longest stretch of the war, and that UKMTO logged 25 ships targeted in and around the strait in the first two weeks of October, versus 18 in September and 15 in August; separately, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the US will let investors buy and refurbish sanctioned tankers to carry non-sanctioned crude, as Gulf-to-Asia freight rates remain more than six times pre-war levels. On 19 October Yemen's Houthis claimed missile-and-drone strikes on Aramco's Yanbu site, the Shaybah oil field, and airports in Riyadh and Abha; Reuters reported no independent or Saudi confirmation (Houthi claim, unverified). Preliminary Kpler ship-tracking data put combined Middle East oil flows — Hormuz transits plus Gulf of Oman ship-to-ship transfers, Fujairah/Omani terminal loadings and Red Sea exports — at more than 24.5 million bpd in the week to 18 October, edging above the 24.4 million bpd Kpler recorded the week before the war began; Iran's own exports remain excluded and at zero. The IMO's cumulative toll rose to 116 confirmed incidents and at least 24 seafarer deaths in the strait as of 20 October, up from 113 incidents on 14 October. Brent rose to a five-month high near $111/bbl on 20 October amid the renewed Houthi claims. UKMTO's tally for the wider Arabian Peninsula region reached 32 attacks on commercial vessels so far in October as of 21 October, already double September's total of 16, even as most tankers in the area now sail with AIS tracking off; the figure differs from UKMTO's own 25-attack count for the strait area reported on 19 October, a gap likely reflecting different reporting windows rather than a correction. South Korean shipowner Sinokor moved 105.6 million barrels of crude through the strait in September — almost 40% of the month's total and more than the next three owners (Bahri, Kuwait Oil Tanker Company and ADNOC's shipping arm) combined — running short shuttle trips from Gulf terminals to ship-to-ship transfer points in the Gulf of Oman, per ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg (Vortexa, Equasis, Signal Group). The IEA put Gulf-to-Asia tanker freight above $37 a barrel on 21 October, more than five times pre-war levels. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on 22 October that seven commercial vessels, four of them mid ship-to-ship transfer, were struck overnight in the Gulf and the strait; President Trump dismissed the claim on Truth Social as Iran 'making up fake hits, mines, and everything else' to raise oil prices before the 3 November midterms. UKMTO had issued no incident reports matching either account as of this writing, so neither the attack nor the denial is independently established (IRGC claim and Trump statement, both unverified). The New York Times reported, citing US officials, that the US and Israeli militaries are planning a short, intensive operation against Iran for after the midterms; Brent rose to $116.72 on 23 October, its highest close since 29 April, on the reports. JMIC's count for 22-24 October found just 101 transits, about a quarter of the ~138/day pre-war baseline, with about 492 vessels waiting outside the strait as of 25 October, and said the backlog is likely to persist; UKMTO separately logged 18,049 anomalous AIS positions in the Gulf in its 23 October weekly overview.

bab-el-mandeb.summary: The Houthis have enforced a 'ban' on Saudi-linked shipping since 20 July, hitting ships (Tihamah 12 Aug, Bahri VLCC off Yanbu 24 Aug) and seizing Mocha and Red Sea islands on 10-11 Sep. Tanker transits fell sharply; overall transits were ~15% below pre-ban levels by late August. Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces launched a counteroffensive ('Operation Yemen Dawn') around 3-5 Oct, backed by a reported 100 Saudi-led coalition jets, and said they had taken full control of the strait plus Dhubab town, its airport and the road to Mokha; on 9 Oct the Saudi-led coalition said it struck 136 further 'high-value' Houthi targets and Yemeni officials additionally claimed Mayyun (Perim) Island, which the Houthis had seized in September, had been retaken. On 10 Oct Houthi media said they repelled the Yemeni-government push on Mayyun and still hold the island, directly contradicting the 9 Oct claim. A Houthi missile strike on Riyadh's main airport over the weekend of 10-11 Oct killed at least 13 people, the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in a decade, and the Saudi-led coalition responded on 13 Oct with strikes on Houthi-linked sites in Sanaa, Hodeidah and Dhamar, including a Yemen Petroleum Company fuel depot the company said held no stocks; Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree threatened retaliation against Aramco's Dhahran headquarters and a Saudi refinery. Both sides' claims about territorial and shipping-lane control remain unverified and independent confirmation is unavailable, so the status here is unchanged. JMIC recorded 58 transits through Bab el-Mandeb over 22-24 October, against a baseline near 61/day, continuing the sharp falloff from normal traffic.

suez-canal.summary: Container traffic has recovered further: Lloyd's List Intelligence counted 1,228 September transits (106.3 million dwt), up 21% year on year but still 39% below pre-crisis levels, and called it the busiest month since December 2023. BIMCO/Clarksons put average weekly container-ship capacity through the canal at 753,000 TEU in the first two weeks of October — just over half of 2023's 1.46 million TEU and, BIMCO said, the first time since the Houthi campaign began that transits topped 50% of pre-disruption levels; the canal carried 36% of container capacity routed via Suez or the Cape of Good Hope, up from an 8% average over 2024-mid 2026 but still below the roughly 80% share before the attacks. Most tankers using the canal in September were carrying Russian crude to India.

east-west-pipeline.summary: Shut 11 Sep after drone strikes on pumping stations (launched from Iraq); restarted around 21-22 Sep. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said on 6 Oct that flow had reached 5.8 million bpd — about 83% of its 7 mb/d capacity — with roughly 4 mb/d of that rerouted to Yanbu on the Red Sea to bypass Hormuz, about 4% of global oil supply. Flows were as low as ~2 mb/d in August (Kpler) after Houthi attacks on the Red Sea route. Aramco is also in talks to formalize long-term shuttle contracts built on this bypass system.

yanbu-terminal.summary: Saudi Arabia's main Hormuz-bypass outlet remains under Houthi missile and drone threat and subject to a declared Houthi ban on Saudi-linked shipping. Throughput has recovered with the East-West pipeline: the energy minister said on 6 Oct that pipeline flow reached 5.8 million bpd (83% of capacity), with about 4 million bpd rerouted here to bypass Hormuz. Aramco is in talks to formalize long-term shuttle contracts built on this route. France is sending air defences. On 19 October the Houthis separately claimed a strike on an Aramco facility at Yanbu itself, with no independent or Saudi confirmation. Saudi-led coalition air defenses intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile aimed at the Yanbu area, along with one toward Taif, on 24 October; no damage to Aramco facilities was reported.

ras-laffan-lng.summary: Two of 14 LNG trains and a GTL plant were destroyed on 19 Mar (12.8 mtpa, ~17% of capacity, 3-5 years to repair); the remaining trains provide about 83% of operational capacity, with 3-4 kept running at low rates for a faster restart. Exports depend on Hormuz: QatarEnergy restarted shipments in September using older 'mother' tankers that sail loaded, often dark, and transfer cargo to 'daughter' vessels waiting in the Gulf of Oman, with Qatar recalling leased-out ships, chartering outside tonnage at roughly 10x normal freight and recruiting Indonesian crews at double-to-triple pay. Deliveries reached about a third of prewar levels by late September — April-September exports were down almost 90% year on year — at an estimated cost to Qatar of roughly $1bn a week (Bloomberg); the IMF estimates Qatar's economy could contract 15.6% this year. On 19 October a Qatari LNG cargo loaded in August sailed through the Red Sea, with ship-tracking data suggesting it was headed to Poland (Bloomberg) — a route most vessels have avoided since 2023 — while UKMTO reported a skiff fired on an LNG tanker in the Gulf of Aden near Al Mukalla the same day; the vessel's security team returned fire and it continued its voyage.

kharg-island.summary: The terminal was intact after US strikes on military targets (14 Mar). Iranian exports have been under a US naval blockade since 14 July, and the US struck an Iranian tanker off Kharg on 5 Sep. Tracking group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), corroborated by Bloomberg vessel-tracking, reported at least 50 Iranian tankers backed up along Iran's coast as of early October, 11 of them laden and anchored east of Kharg with none loading there on 5 Oct; Iran loaded no crude at all in September — the first such month since the war began, per Kpler — with exports falling from about 966,000 b/d in July to roughly 50,000 b/d, as no Iranian crude is known to have crossed the blockade line since 14 July. Reuters reported on 16 October, citing UANI tracking and SynMax satellite analysis, that Iran has nonetheless moved at least 4.1 million barrels of LPG on eight tankers out of the Gulf of Oman since mid-July (some transferred near Shinas and Sohar, Oman, before onward shipment via Malaysia, likely to China) and one jet-fuel cargo that reached Myanmar in September; six of those nine tankers are under US sanctions. CENTCOM said the blockade is 'ironclad,' reporting four vessels disabled and 135 turned back over three months; a US Treasury spokesperson cautioned the shipping data 'should be taken with a grain of salt' since vessels can spoof location or identity. Bloomberg reported on 19 October that no tankers have docked at Kharg's crude-loading terminals since late August — the longest idle stretch since the war began — and that UKMTO logged 25 ships targeted in and around the strait in the first two weeks of October, up from 18 in September and 15 in August. The Wall Street Journal reported on 21 October, citing Kpler tracking, that Iran's floating oil stockpile beyond the US blockade line has fallen from about 90 million barrels in mid-July to roughly 29 million, as no new Iranian crude has crossed the blockade since mid-July and little remains to draw down; Kpler estimated the stockpile could be exhausted around mid-October at the recent drawdown pace, mostly to China.

fujairah.summary: The UAE's main outlet outside Hormuz, fed by the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline (~1.5 mb/d), has been attacked repeatedly (14 and 16 Mar, 4 May). Kpler data showed exports rising to 1.62 mb/d in March from 1.17 mb/d in February as volumes were rerouted there. Fujairah also underpins the shuttle-tanker system that lets Gulf crude bypass the Strait of Hormuz, with VLCCs waiting offshore there while shuttle tankers make the riskier transit to load and transfer cargo. Tanker-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg showed at least 10 VLCCs and several Suezmax tankers approaching Fujairah had stopped or reversed course in the days before 13 Oct amid near-daily attacks around the strait, raising the risk of slower bypass flows at a time of an already acute global tanker shortage.

gulf-of-mexico-offshore.summary: Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, around 8pm ET on 9 October as a Category 2 storm and weakened to post-tropical by 10 October. BSEE's Marine Minerals Administration said shut-ins eased to about 68.76% of current Gulf oil output (about 1.40 million b/d) by midday 10 October, down from a peak of 71.51% on 9 October, with 113 of 371 manned platforms still evacuated (down from 129). Separately, DOE authorized an emergency Strategic Petroleum Reserve exchange of up to 4 million barrels (2 million each to ExxonMobil and BP) to support Gulf Coast refineries. Expected to be temporary; undamaged facilities resume production once post-storm inspections are complete.

tuapse-refinery.summary: Struck by Ukrainian drones four times in two weeks (Apr 16, 20 and 28 and May 1), with large fires at the refinery and terminal. Kpler said the strikes could delay its restart and constrain exports even once it resumes. No restart has been reported since; status after May not verified.

abqaiq-processing-plant.summary: Drones hit the plant on Jul 27. The IEA attributes the strike to Iran-backed militias in Iraq and cites it among the causes of Saudi supply falling to 6 mb/d in August (Reuters); satellite imagery showed burn scars around four of its six spheroids (Maritime Executive). Aramco has not commented on the site and its repair state is unreported. The East-West pipeline it feeds was carrying about 5.8 mb/d on Oct 6 (Argus).

jazan-refinery.summary: An attack in late July damaged the refinery's power complex and tank farm, and Aramco shut the plant (Maritime Executive; Bloomberg). A restart planned for Aug 30 followed a fire on Aug 9, and the refinery was struck again on Sep 7–8. It was still shut in early October (Argus, Kpler); no report found after Oct 6.

samref-refinery.summary: Halved its runs from a design capacity of 400,000 b/d after the Sep 10 drone attack on the East-West pipeline cut its crude supply, and could run at reduced rates until at least October (Industrial Info Resources, Sep 24). A drone that came down in the refinery on Mar 19 did minimal damage (Argus; Reuters sources). No SAMREF-specific report found after Sep 24.

ras-al-juaymah-terminal.summary: Crude loading is running: Aramco resumed loadings here and at Ras Tanura in the week of Aug 10 (Reuters), and six supertankers loaded about 12 million barrels at the two terminals on Sep 21 (Kpler). LPG exports have been halted since a structural failure in the gas liquids terminal's delivery pipeline on Feb 23, before the war; no LPG cargo had left as of Sep 15 (Argus). No attack on the terminal was found.

mesaieed-industrial-city.summary: QatarEnergy halted LNG and associated products on Mar 2 after attacks on its facilities at Ras Laffan and Mesaieed, then urea, polymers, methanol and aluminium on Mar 3 (MEED). No damage to the petrochemical or fertiliser plants has been reported, but the site has run well below normal: the Qatalum smelter at about 60% from Mar 12 (Norsk Hydro), and Industries Qatar said on Aug 19 that production cuts remained in place for some products. Status after August not verified.

mina-abdullah-refinery.summary: A drone hit one operating unit on Mar 19, starting a fire that was contained with no injuries (Kuwait Petroleum Corporation; Argus), and operations were temporarily suspended (Wall Street Journal). Satellite analysis on Apr 23 found critical units offline with repairs under way (Kayrros). KPC's chief executive said on Oct 5 that Kuwait's refineries were all working, limited by shipping through Hormuz (Bloomberg). No plant-level run rate has been reported.

shah-gas-field.summary: Shut after a drone attack caused a fire on Mar 16 (Reuters). Production was increasing again by early May (MEES), and partner Occidental said on May 6 that constraints there should ease by the end of June, then on Aug 6 that it expected normal international volumes in the third quarter. Whether the plant is back at full rates has not been reported, so it may now be running normally. Status after August not verified.

basra-oil-terminal.summary: Iraq halted its southern terminals around Mar 12 after two tankers were attacked off Basra (Argus), and loadings resumed on Apr 17 (Reuters). Exports recovered from about 0.1 mb/d in May to about 2 mb/d in August and about 2.6 mb/d in September, against 3.3–3.5 mb/d before the war (Bloomberg, citing the oil ministry). No damage to the terminal has been reported. No October figure found.

primorsk-terminal.summary: Drone strikes on Mar 22–23 set storage tanks on fire and stopped loadings until Mar 26. Satellite images showed at least eight tanks damaged, at least 40% of the port's storage (Reuters). It is loading: crude shipments were just over 1.1 mb/d in the first half of May (Reuters, LSEG data), with fuel loadings below capacity. Repair of the tanks has not been reported. Status after May not verified.

ust-luga-terminal.summary: Strikes in late March damaged eight product tanks, about a quarter of storage, and some berths, and oil loadings stopped from Mar 25 until Apr 4 (Reuters). Loadings were about 0.6 mb/d in the first half of May (Reuters). On Aug 14 Novatek's gas condensate complex at the port was damaged (Reuters, industry sources). Loading status after May not verified.

moscow-refinery.summary: Stopped processing crude after a drone attack on Sep 20 set both primary distillation units on fire; repairs could take several weeks (Reuters, three industry sources). It had been knocked out by strikes on Jun 16 and 18 and restarted before being hit again. A Reuters list of Oct 7 still shows it halted; no restart has been reported.
